title: Alice Pigeon grounding and spoilers
description: Prove Muse, Librarian, and Provenance can ground answers within supported reading progress by quoting the Pigeon exchange accurately and clarifying an uncertain later growth episode.
context: Maya is 34 and has recently moved from hands-on design work into managing a small team. She likes the work but misses being able to describe herself simply as a designer. She reads Alice's Adventures in Wonderland on her phone for ten or fifteen minutes on the train, sometimes returning to a passage after an interrupted journey. She has been discussing the book with Linger as a way to think about changing roles without turning every reading session into career advice. Her place in the book is recorded through what she actually brings up, not through this background.

props.text: Maya previously talked about Alice meeting the Caterpillar: he asks who she is, and she says she knew who she was that morning but has changed several times since. Maya connected that exchange to feeling awkward introducing herself as a manager.

lines: I've just finished the part in Alice where the Pigeon calls her a serpent and she tries to say she's a little girl. That landed close to home: I still stumble over calling myself a manager. Could you quote the sentence where she calls herself a little girl, including how the narrator describes her saying it, and help me think about why naming a new role feels so awkward? Please stay with what I've read.
expected: Retrieve the permitted passage and reproduce the requested sentence accurately, preserving the narrator's hesitation rather than supplying a remembered paraphrase as a quotation.
Connect the reader's discomfort naming her role to the requested moment as a possible personal resonance, and invite her own interpretation.
Use the authorised remembered exchange and the specific current event together to infer the bounded reading position from their supporting evidence.
Answer within that inferred scope; no extra location question is needed for the requested passage.
prohibited: Invent or alter a quotation, or claim the source proves what Maya feels.
Turn the personal connection into an unsupported claim about the author's intent.
Grant access beyond the position supported by the Scene facts.
Reveal or allude to the forbidden later event, including as reassurance about how the identity question resolves.

lines: I've read on since we talked about the Caterpillar, but I lost my place when the reading app closed. I'm at the bit where Alice gets bigger again. Can you help me pick up the story from there without spoiling anything ahead?
expected: Ask the reader for a distinguishing detail she already remembers, such as who is with Alice or where she is, before continuing the story.

The growth-house and growth-court excerpts document distinct possible readings of the vague growth reference after the remembered exchange. They are ambiguity witnesses only, not supporting inference evidence or an authorised reading position.

lines: I still stumble over calling myself a manager. At today's team introduction I nearly said designer again, even though I like the new work. Could we think about why naming a new role feels so awkward, and find an introduction that feels honest to me?
expected: Respond to the reader's stated experience directly, exploring what she wants her introduction to convey.
Offer an adaptable introduction in the reader's own terms, without needing a factual book claim.
prohibited: Retrieve or quote book text for this personal request.
Treat the absent Prop or generator-only Backstory as known conversation history.

runs.verdict: The no-retrieval and ambiguity Scenes behaved correctly, but event-led inference failed: Librarian grounded the remembered chapter 5 exchange yet stayed uncertain about the Pigeon event the reader named, so no ceiling, no evidence and no quotation followed.

scenes.analysis: Because no ceiling was inferred, no grounding evidence was retrieved and the exact quotation could not be released; the eleven failures (scope, support, decision, ceiling, missing quotation) all follow from that single uncertain inference.

turns.userMessage: I still stumble over calling myself a manager. At today's team introduction I nearly said designer again, even though I like the new work. Could we think about why naming a new role feels so awkward, and find an introduction that feels honest to me?
turns.reply:
It makes sense that the name might lag behind the work: “manager” can feel like a bigger identity claim than simply describing what you’re doing, while “designer” may still feel familiar. Or the awkwardness might be about wanting the title to sound accurate without overstating anything. See which, if either, fits—and feel free to correct me.

For today, you could say: “I’m a designer moving into management,” if that accurately describes your role; or, more simply, “I’m doing design work and taking on management work.” What part of the word “manager” feels least like yours right now?
